title: Perforated Peptic Ulcer
description: Diagnose with CT, start antibiotics and operate without delay, pick the approach by physiology, repair by ulcer size and site, and prevent recurrence.
objectives: Diagnose perforation with CT when it is promptly available
Start broad-spectrum antibiotics and operate without delay
Choose laparoscopy for stable patients and open surgery for unstable ones
Repair small ulcers primarily; resect suspicious gastric ulcers with frozen section
Keep postoperative antibiotics short and eradicate H. pylori

references.citation: Tarasconi A, Coccolini F, Biffl WL, et al. Perforated and bleeding peptic ulcer: WSES guidelines. World J Emerg Surg. 2020;15:3.

Ng EK, Lam YH, Sung JJ, et al. Eradication of Helicobacter pylori prevents recurrence of ulcer after simple closure of duodenal ulcer perforation: randomized controlled trial. Ann Surg. 2000;231(2):153-158.
Kamada T, Satoh K, Itoh T, et al. Evidence-based clinical practice guidelines for peptic ulcer disease 2020. J Gastroenterol. 2021;56(4):303-322.
Sawyer RG, Claridge JA, Nathens AB, et al. Trial of short-course antimicrobial therapy for intraabdominal infection. N Engl J Med. 2015;372(21):1996-2005.

start.text: A 64-year-old man who takes ibuprofen daily for knee pain has 5 hours of sudden, severe epigastric pain that is now generalized. The abdomen is rigid.

imaging.text: CT is immediately available. What imaging?

options.label: Upright chest X-ray only; no free air rules out perforation
options.feedback: Free air is seen on plain films in only 30–85% of perforations, so a negative film does not rule out perforation. WSES 2020 (strong, 1C): CT for suspected perforated peptic ulcer, with chest/abdominal X-ray as the initial study only if CT is not promptly available.

options.label: CT of the abdomen and pelvis
options.feedback: WSES 2020 (strong, 1C): CT for suspected perforated peptic ulcer. Plain X-ray is the fallback only when CT is not promptly available, because free air is detected in just 30–85% of cases.

ct_result.text: CT: pneumoperitoneum and free fluid around the stomach and duodenum, consistent with a perforated peptic ulcer. No contained or sealed collection.

initial.text: Initial management: which belong in your plan?

options.label: Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics now
IV fluid resuscitation and analgesia
Book the operating room without delay
Non-operative trial with a PPI and antibiotics; operate if he worsens
Wait for the morning list; he is not in shock
Routine empirical antifungal therapy

initial.feedback: WSES 2020: start empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics as soon as possible (1C) and operate as soon as possible (1B); in a Danish cohort each hour of delay cut the adjusted probability of survival by 2.4%. Non-operative management is not routine and is reserved for extremely selected sealed perforations confirmed on a water-soluble contrast study (2C). Antifungals are only for high-risk patients (2C).

stable.text: In the operating room he remains hemodynamically stable, and you have the laparoscopic skills and equipment. Approach?

options.label: Endoscopic clipping of the perforation
options.feedback: WSES 2020 (weak, 2C): avoid endoscopic treatment such as clipping, fibrin glue sealing, or stenting for perforated peptic ulcer. Clips may not hold in fibrotic ulcer tissue that has lost its compliance.

options.label: Laparoscopic repair
options.feedback: WSES 2020 (weak, 2B): in stable patients, a laparoscopic approach, with open surgery if laparoscopic skills or equipment are lacking.

unstable.text: On induction he becomes hypotensive and needs escalating norepinephrine. What approach?

options.label: Open laparotomy, with a damage-control strategy if his physiology keeps deteriorating
options.feedback: WSES 2020: open surgery for unstable patients (strong, 1D), and a damage-control strategy in septic shock with severe physiological derangement (weak, 2D).

options.label: Laparoscopic repair as planned
options.feedback: WSES 2020 (strong, 1D): unstable patients should have open surgery. Pneumoperitoneum raises PaCO2 and reduces venous return, stroke volume, and cardiac output, which precludes laparoscopy in hemodynamically unstable patients.

duodenal_repair.text: At operation: a 7 mm perforation of the anterior duodenal bulb with healthy edges. How do you repair it?

options.label: Primary closure, with or without an omental patch
options.feedback: WSES 2020 (weak, 2C): primary repair for perforations smaller than 2 cm; no recommendation can be made on whether an omental patch adds protection. Ng 2000: with H. pylori eradication, immediate acid-reduction surgery is unnecessary.

options.label: Distal gastrectomy for definitive ulcer control
options.feedback: WSES 2020 (weak, 2C): primary repair for perforations smaller than 2 cm. Ng 2000: after simple closure, H. pylori eradication prevented ulcer relapse, and immediate acid-reduction surgery was unnecessary even with generalized peritonitis.

gastric_ulcer.text: At operation: a 2.5 cm perforation on the lesser curve of the stomach with rolled, indurated edges. How do you manage it?

options.label: Simple closure; biopsy is unnecessary in an emergency
options.feedback: A large perforated gastric ulcer can be a perforated cancer. WSES 2020: for large gastric ulcers suspicious for malignancy, resection with intraoperative frozen section whenever possible.

options.label: Resection with intraoperative frozen-section pathology where possible
options.feedback: WSES 2020: tailor repair of perforations over 2 cm to the ulcer's location. For large gastric ulcers suspicious for malignancy, resection with intraoperative frozen-section examination whenever possible.

postop_antibiotics.text: Source control has been achieved. How long do antibiotics continue?

options.label: A short course: 3–5 days, or until inflammatory markers normalize
options.feedback: WSES 2020 (weak, 2C): a short course of antibiotics, 3–5 days or until inflammatory markers normalize, after perforated peptic ulcer. In STOP-IT, about 4 days of fixed therapy after adequate source control gave outcomes similar to longer courses.

options.label: Two weeks of IV antibiotics
options.feedback: WSES 2020 (weak, 2C): a short course, 3–5 days or until inflammatory markers normalize. In STOP-IT, about 4 days of fixed therapy after adequate source control was as effective as courses running up to 10 days.

recurrence.text: Before discharge, what prevents a recurrent ulcer?

options.label: A 4-week PPI course alone
options.feedback: Ng 2000: after simple closure of an H. pylori-positive duodenal perforation, 1-year ulcer relapse was 38.1% with omeprazole alone vs 4.8% after eradication therapy.

options.label: Test for H. pylori and give eradication therapy if positive, and stop the NSAID
options.feedback: Ng 2000 (RCT): eradicating H. pylori after simple closure cut 1-year relapse from 38.1% (omeprazole alone) to 4.8%. For NSAID-induced ulcers, the NSAID is discontinued (JSGE 2020), so his daily ibuprofen stops.

fail_missed.text: Diagnostic Error: Perforation missed on plain films.

fail_delay.text: Complication: Worsening peritonitis and sepsis from delayed source control.

fail_endoscopic.text: Guideline Deviation: Endoscopic closure without peritoneal source control.

fail_overtreatment.text: Management Error: Gastric resection for a small duodenal perforation.

fail_missed_cancer.text: Diagnostic Risk: Possible perforated gastric cancer closed without tissue.

fail_duration.text: Guideline Deviation: Prolonged antibiotics after source control.

fail_recurrence.text: Complication: Recurrent ulcer within a year.

success.text: Procedure Complete: Perforation repaired, H. pylori treated, NSAID stopped.
